idiom_name: struct embedding (embedded field) with compiler-promoted methods; override a promoted method to specialise
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance, and delegation is the language's reuse mechanism: an embedded field's methods are promoted into the struct's method set by the compiler, so `type countingStore struct { Store }` satisfies `Store` without a single forwarding function, and an outer method with the same name overrides the promoted one. Because promotion is all-or-nothing, embedding exposes the delegate's entire method set - hide the field (hold a named, unexported field and write the two or three methods you want) when the wrapper should be narrower. Embed a pointer when the embedded type has pointer-receiver methods or may be nil; embedding by value copies the delegate, which is usually wrong for stateful delegates.
pitfalls: Promotion is all-or-nothing: every exported method of the embedded type becomes part of the wrapper's API, so embedding is not a way to narrow an interface - use a named field plus a small interface for that.

Self-calls inside the embedded type do not re-enter the wrapper: a promoted method that calls another method of the embedded type runs the embedded implementation, not the wrapper's override, so overriding one member does not change the delegate's internal behaviour.
Embedding two types (or a type and its pointer) with a same-named method makes selection a compile-time ambiguous-selector error, and calling promoted methods through a nil embedded pointer panics.
